datasets.label: NCMEC CyberTipline reports of suspected online child sexual exploitation, 2020–2025
datasets.publisher: National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC)
datasets.underlying_model: Administrative count of reports received — not a statistical model
datasets.definition: Reports of suspected child sexual exploitation received by NCMEC's CyberTipline during each calendar year. Reports come from the public and, for US-based electronic service providers, under the mandatory reporting duty in 18 USC 2258A, which covers apparent child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and — since the REPORT Act took effect in 2024 — online enticement and child sex trafficking. The unit is a REPORT, not a child: one child can appear in many reports and one report can contain many files, incidents and users. Country is assigned from geographic indicators for the reported incident (typically the upload location), not the victim's location.
datasets.value_type_note: A counted tally of reports actually received, published to the unit by the organisation that receives them. It is not a survey, an estimate or a model, so there is no uncertainty interval — but it is a count of REPORTING, which is not the same as a count of abuse. It measures what platforms detected and chose to report, so it moves with detection technology, platform policy and law as well as with underlying harm.
datasets.uncertainty: None published, and none applicable: this is a count, not an estimate. The relevant limitation is coverage, not sampling error — see comparability_warnings.

comparability_warnings.warning: Totals fell from 36.2m to 21.2m reports. NCMEC attributes this partly to a new 'bundling' feature that consolidates many incidents from one viral event into a single report, and partly to reduced submissions from some providers and the spread of end-to-end encryption. The drop therefore reflects changes in how reports are counted and made, and must not be read as a fall in online child sexual exploitation.

From 2024 NCMEC splits reports into 'referrals' and 'informational' reports, and the REPORT Act added online enticement and child sex trafficking to mandatory reporting. The series shown is total reports (referrals + informational) so that all years use the same definition.

datasets.country_attribution_warning: NCMEC states explicitly that country-specific numbers are NOT indicative of the level of child sexual abuse in a particular country. Figures are affected by proxies, VPNs and anonymisers, by each country's own laws when assessing content, and by the fact that a report attributed to one country may involve offenders or victims elsewhere. Larger numbers most often reflect a larger online population and more detection by providers, not a more dangerous country.
datasets.licence: NCMEC publishes these reports publicly for awareness and policy use. NCMEC does not endorse eRaksha or this presentation. See docs/DATA_AUDIT.md.

context.statement: NCMEC: reports to the CyberTipline in 2024 contained 62,992,859 files (images, videos and other material), including 33,130,449 video files uploaded by reporting providers.
context.comparability: Files are a different unit from reports and from children. One report can contain thousands of files, and the same file can appear in many reports, so files must never be compared with or added to report counts.

context.statement: NCMEC: the 20.5 million reports received in 2024 related to 29.2 million incidents of suspected child sexual exploitation.
context.comparability: Incidents exceed reports because one bundled report can carry many incidents. The incident count is published for 2024 only, so this app uses reports — the measure available for every year — as its series, and does not mix the two.

context.statement: NCMEC (2024): the CyberTipline received nearly 100 reports of financial sextortion per day.
context.comparability: A subset of total reports, published as an approximate daily average by NCMEC. Quoted as published; not recomputed and not added to the main series.

context.statement: WHO/Europe (25 September 2024): problematic social media use rose from 7% (2018) to 11% (2022) among adolescents aged 11, 13 and 15 across 44 countries and regions in Europe, central Asia and Canada (HBSC survey).
context.underlying_model: Health Behaviour in School-aged Children survey (self-report)
context.comparability: A regional self-reported measure of a usage pattern among adolescents. It is a different population, unit and source from the CyberTipline counts, so it is never combined with them; it is shown only as separate context on online wellbeing.
